title: Not to be served (Mark 10:32–45)
hook: James and John want the best seats; he came to serve and give his life
carry: not to be served, but to serve

segments.voice: Yesterday, a camel and a needle, and the line all things are possible. What did you manage to give away? Day two hundred four.

They're on the road going up to Jerusalem now, and Jesus is walking out in front. Mark says the disciples were amazed, and the ones following were afraid. He takes the twelve aside and tells them, for the third time and in the most detail yet: he'll be condemned, handed over to the Romans, mocked, spat on, flogged and killed, and after three days rise. And right then, James and John come up to him with a request. Their opening line is every kid asking a parent to agree before hearing the question. "Master, we would that thou shouldest do for us whatsoever we shall desire." What is it? Let us sit, one on your right and one on your left, in your glory. The best seats. Reserved.
screen: `ON THE ROAD UP TO JERUSALEM.` → `A THIRD WARNING.` → `SAVE US THE BEST SEATS.`

segments.voice: Jesus answers them: you don't know what you're asking. Can you drink the cup I drink? We can, they say, quickly. And he says: you will. But the seats aren't mine to give. When the other ten hear about it, they're furious, probably because they didn't think of asking first. So Jesus calls them all together. You know how rulers among the nations lord it over people, and the powerful throw their weight around. But it shall not be so among you. Whoever wants to be great must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all. And then the sentence many call the key to Mark's whole gospel: "For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." Ministered unto means served. He came not to be served, but to serve. And today's word, ransom. In Greek, lytron: the price paid to set someone free, a captive or a slave. Everybody in that world knew what it meant to be bought out. Christians have understood this word in different ways. Many hear it as the heart of the cross: Jesus's death sets people free from sin. Theologians have argued for centuries about who, if anyone, is paid; many say the picture is about the cost of freedom, not a bill handed to someone. What every reading keeps is the direction: the one who could claim the top seat spends himself for others. A few chapters on, Mark will show who ends up on his right and his left. It won't be what James and John had in mind.
screen: `CAN YE DRINK OF THE CUP?` · `IT SHALL NOT BE SO AMONG YOU.` · `NOT TO BE SERVED, BUT TO SERVE.` · `RANSOM: THE PRICE OF FREEDOM.` · then, large: `TO GIVE HIS LIFE A RANSOM FOR MANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to take the lowest seat. Settle, and breathe. Picture a place you'll be today. A table, a meeting, a car, a line. Where's the best seat, the first turn, the last word? Now picture yourself choosing the other one, on purpose, without making a show of it. The back of the line. The middle seat. Serving the food before sitting down. Feel what that's like. If you pray, you can offer it as a small way of following. The bell holds the time.
Ransom. In Greek, lytron: the price paid to set a captive free. He came to give his life as a ransom for many.
Your line: not to be served, but to serve. Today, take the lowest seat once, and don't tell anyone why. Day two hundred four.

howItsDone: Christians often call Mark 10:45 a summary of Jesus's mission, and many churches describe their ministries of service with its words; some leaders wash feet or serve meals to others as a sign of it.

original.note: Greek: a ransom, the price paid to free a captive or a slave. from lyō, to loose.

trapdoor: what you thought: ransom is money kidnappers demand.
what it means: the price that sets someone free; Jesus says he came to serve and give his life that way, for many.
what a scholar hears: lytron, from lyō, to loose. and who is paid has been argued since the early church.

notes: 'The other ten were furious, probably because they didn't think of asking first' is light humor, not in the text. Keeper may cut.

Atonement readings kept general: ransom from sin; the long debate over to whom a ransom is paid (early ransom-to-the-devil views; Anselm and others rejecting them). Confirm fairness to Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers.
Forward hint to Mark 15:27 (two crucified on his right and left) is left unstated. Confirm acceptable.
'Many call the key to Mark's whole gospel' for 10:45 is a common scholarly description; confirm.
